newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela bolsters dream of revived African diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Mandela bolsters dream of revived African diplomacy.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela failed to deliver the measured transfer of power in Kinshasa that was his wish, but he has gone a long way towards the renaissance of African diplomacy he dreams of.

Praise for Mandela's diplomacy in the renamed Democratic Republic of Congo has come from world leaders including U.S. President Bill Clinton and from analysts across the continent he seeks to put back on the path to growth and stability.

"Mr Mandela of South Africa has done a superb job of exercising leadership in this area...I want the whole world to get behind the leadership that Nelson Mandela is showing there," Clinton said last week.

Some African diplomats privately call Mandela naive, but they concede that his ceaseless efforts to achieve and maintain unity amongst African and Western leaders towards the former Zaire helped to limit the violence of the transfer of power from Mobuu Sese Seko to Laurent Kabila.
"He was there at the forefront, listening, making suggestions, counselling, consulting fellow African leaders and nudging the process forward," said Zimbabwean political analyst Lupi Mashayakarara.
"That is what leadership is all about," he said.

Kabila foiled Mandela's plan to make him and then-president Mobutu adopt his 10-point programme for a peaceful transition to democracy last week when he refused to board a South African ship for peace talks.

But Mandela's spokesman, Joel Netshitenzhe, said on Monday Mandela would continue to advise Kabila to follow essentially the same programme towards lasting democracy and stability in African's third largest country.

He said Mandela's efforts in Zaire and his record of peace making in Angola, Lesotho and Swaziland would "conjecturally" bolster the country's claim to a Security Council seat when the United Nations implements restructuring plans still being made.

"The peace process was a disappointment, but President Mandela still holds the moral high ground," said Willie Breytenbach of the Stellenbosch Centre for African Studies. "South Africa has established itself as the major diplomatic power of Africa."
Vernon Seymour of the University Of the Western Cape said South Africa had established the credentials for a leading role in the global diplomacy of peacemaking and crisis prevention.
"Clearly these are the kind of credentials that would be needed for the African representative on an expanded Security Council," he said.

For the first two years after he had led South Africa from apartheid to democracy, Mandela, now 78, took a back seat in African diplomacy, calling always for a collective response to the continent's crises and challenges.

But he signalled a change of heart last year when he rejected a proposal by outgoing U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher for an African crisis-intervention force trained and partly financed by Western powers, but manned by Africans.
He told Christopher that Africa would in future reject outside interventions and seek to controlling its own destiny.
On Tuesday, Mandela reinforced his theme when he told neighbouring Zimbabwe's parliament he had tried to find a truly African solution for an African problem in the former Zaire.
"The time has come for Africa to take full responsibility for her woes, use the immense collective wisdom it possesses to make a reality of the ideal of the African renaissance whose time has come.

"It is a renaissance that must mean that Africa refuses to be a passive onlooker in a changing world, hapless victim to modern machinations of the forces historically responsible for her woes," he said.
Breytenbach said the failure of other African leaders to publicly and loudly support Mandela's search for peace in Zaire had been the greatest disappointment of the past weeks.
"It was supposed to be an African initiative, but in the end it was a bilateral affair between South Africa and the United States," he said.
Netshitenzhe disagreed, saying Mandela had consulted the United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity and African leaders throughout his attempt to broker a Zairean peace.
Seymour said that while Mandela had acted in conjunction with other African states, he had been left to do the work.
"Although it was essentially an African initiative, the bulk of the foot-soldiering was done by South Africa," he said.
